title: What an API Is and Why It Exists
learningObjectives: Explain the key ideas and terminology of what an api is and why it exists.
Recognize how the concept is used in real software communication.
Identify common mistakes or risks associated with this topic.
Apply the concept to a small, fictional API scenario.
Review a communication design and justify appropriate choices.

understand.concept: An API (Application Programming Interface) is a defined way for software components to request capabilities or exchange information. It specifies available operations, expected inputs, outputs, and rules. APIs can be local libraries, operating-system services, or network services. An API is a contract between components—not necessarily a website or a single technology.
understand.whyItMatters: APIs let programs reuse capabilities without needing to know every internal detail of the component providing them.
understand.analogy: Think of a delivery process with a sender, a message, and a receiver who returns a confirmation or explanation.
understand.analogyLimit: Software communication may involve complex protocols, asynchronous timing, security, and partial failures that this everyday analogy cannot fully capture.

explain.narrative:
An API (Application Programming Interface) is a defined way for software components to request capabilities or exchange information. It specifies available operations, expected inputs, outputs, and rules. APIs can be local libraries, operating-system services, or network services. An API is a contract between components—not necessarily a website or a single technology.

Use the protocol and service documentation as the authoritative guide for a real API. Examples here are conceptual and intentionally do not make live network calls.

examples.title: Describe an API contract
examples.explanation: A contract names an operation and describes what it accepts and returns.

examples.title: Call a local function API
examples.explanation: A function can expose an API to other code in the same program.

examples.title: Use a returned value
examples.explanation: The caller reads the value defined by the component's contract.

examples.title: Document failure behavior
examples.explanation: An API contract should describe expected failure outcomes too.

examples.title: Compare implementation and interface
examples.explanation: Callers use the interface rather than depending on hidden internals.

commonMistakes: Assuming every request succeeds or returns the same shape.
Treating parsing as validation or authentication as authorization.
Ignoring timeout, rate-limit, and failure responses.
Embedding secret credentials in public client code.
Retrying operations without considering duplicate side effects.
